chapters.title: Chapter 5: Evaluating Startups and Building Your Portfolio

lessons.title: How Much to Allocate and How Many Startups to Back

children.text: Two friends in Hyderabad each decide to become angels. Sameer puts ₹50 lakh into two startups run by people he knows, in a single month. Anjali sets aside ₹20 lakh, backs 14 startups over four years, and keeps part of the money for follow-on rounds in whichever companies pull ahead. Sameer's outcome depends almost entirely on luck. Anjali's has a real chance of catching a winner and surviving the failures. Everything you learned about failure rates and the power law comes down to three practical decisions: how much to put into startups in total, how many companies to back, and how big each cheque should be. This lesson turns those decisions into simple, repeatable maths.

body.text: Decide your total budget first, then the number of companies, then the cheque size. The order matters: cheque size is the output of a plan, not the place to start.

children.text: Step 1: Are You Ready to Invest in Startups at All?

body.title: Readiness checklist before any angel cheque
steps: I have an emergency fund covering at least six months of expenses, kept separately from investments.
I have adequate term life and health insurance for myself and my dependants.
I have no high-interest debt, such as credit card dues or personal loans.
My retirement savings and big goals, like children's education, are funded or on track.
I will not need this money for at least 7 to 10 years.
I can lose every rupee of it without changing my lifestyle or my plans.

body.text: If you cannot tick every box, the right angel budget today is zero. Startups will still exist in two years. A missing emergency fund or an unfunded goal is a much more certain problem than a missed startup opportunity.

children.text: Step 2: Set Your Total Angel Budget

markDefs.definition: Financial assets you control and could reasonably invest or sell, such as bank deposits, mutual funds, shares and bonds. It excludes your own home and money locked away for specific needs.

children.text: A guideline commonly cited by experienced angels is to keep total startup exposure to around 5 to 10% of your
, with first-timers starting at the lower end. It is a guardrail, not a target: nobody has to invest 5% in startups.

body.caption: The budget covers everything over several years: initial cheques, follow-ons and any fees.

body.title: Set the budget
body.prompt: Divya's investable net worth is ₹2.4 crore. She decides to allocate 7.5% to angel investing over the next four years. What is her total angel budget, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹2.4 crore × 7.5% = ₹240 lakh × 0.075 = ₹18 lakh. That ₹18 lakh has to cover every initial cheque, every follow-on and any fees for the next several years, not just this year's deals.

children.text: Step 3: Decide How Many Companies to Back

In Chapter 3 you saw that the chance of owning at least one big winner is 1 − (1 − p)ᴺ, where p is the chance any one startup becomes a big winner and N is the number of startups. The table shows why a handful of cheques is closer to a lottery ticket than a portfolio.

body.caption: Chance of owning at least one big winner (illustrative probabilities per startup)

body.label: Common portfolio size guidance
body.value: 15 to 25 or more companies, built over 3 to 5 years
body.context: This is a widely used rule of thumb rather than a precise number. Fewer companies means your result depends more heavily on luck.

children.text: Step 4: Split Initial Cheques and Reserves

markDefs.definition: The part of your angel budget held back to invest again in later rounds of your best-performing portfolio companies.

children.text: Many angels hold back a share of their budget as
, often somewhere between 30% and 50%, to use pro-rata rights in the companies that are clearly pulling ahead. The rest is split across initial cheques.

body.caption: Example: ₹30 lakh budget, 40% reserves, 20 companies. ₹30 lakh × 0.6 = ₹18 lakh for initial cheques, so ₹90,000 per company.

body.text: The maths often collides with reality. ₹90,000 may be below the minimum cheque that a syndicate, a founder or a platform will accept. When that happens, you have three honest options: back fewer companies and accept more luck-dependence, build the portfolio more slowly as your budget grows, or use a structure such as a fund that pools small commitments, if you are eligible. What you should not do is quietly raise the budget to fit the minimums.

body.title: Size the initial cheque
body.prompt: Rohan has an angel budget of ₹50 lakh. He keeps 30% in reserve for follow-ons and plans to back 14 companies. How big is each initial cheque, in ₹ lakh?
body.explanation: ₹50 lakh × (1 − 0.30) = ₹35 lakh for initial cheques. ₹35 lakh ÷ 14 = ₹2.5 lakh per company. The remaining ₹15 lakh is held back for follow-on rounds in his strongest companies.

body.title: Building your own portfolio vs pooling through a fund

points: Full control over which companies you back

children.text: Step 5: Pace It Over Several Years

Startup valuations move in cycles. Angels who deployed their whole budget during the 2021 funding boom paid peak prices, and many of those companies struggled to raise again in the slowdown that followed. Spreading initial cheques across three to five years means you buy in good and bad markets, just as a SIP spreads your purchases across market levels. Here is how Rohan might pace his ₹50 lakh:

body.title: Rohan's illustrative deployment plan (₹ lakh per year)

body.label: The follow-on rule
body.value: Reserves are for winners, not rescues
body.context: Use follow-on money where a company has hit its milestones and is raising at a higher valuation from credible investors. Using reserves to prop up a struggling company is how angels turn one loss into two.

body.text: Watch for concentration drift. If one company succeeds, your stake in it can grow to a large share of your net worth, far above the 5 to 10% you planned. At that point, a partial secondary sale is not a lack of conviction; it can be sensible risk management.

body.title: Which plan is sound?
body.question: Four investors each have ₹1 crore of investable net worth and have ticked every box on the readiness checklist. Whose angel plan best reflects this lesson?
options: Kiran invests ₹25 lakh in one friend's startup this month
Leela invests ₹8 lakh across 8 startups over three years and keeps ₹2 lakh for follow-ons
Mohit invests ₹10 lakh in 20 startups in a single week during a hot market
Nisha borrows ₹10 lakh to back 10 startups because she is confident in her picks
body.explanation: Leela stays within 10% of investable net worth, spreads cheques across several companies and years, and holds reserves. Kiran is concentrated and oversized, Mohit ignores timing risk by deploying everything at once in a hot market, and borrowing to invest in startups, as Nisha plans, turns a possible total loss into debt.

body.title: Harsh's plan
body.scenario: Harsh, 38, is a chartered accountant in Ahmedabad with an investable net worth of ₹1.6 crore, a home loan and two young children. His emergency fund and insurance are in place. Excited by a friend's success, he wants to put ₹40 lakh into four startups from his personal network this year.
body.prompt: What is wrong with the plan, and what would a more disciplined version look like?
body.modelAnswer:
1. Too much: ₹40 lakh is 25% of his investable net worth, well above the commonly cited 5 to 10% range, which works out to ₹8 lakh to ₹16 lakh.
2. Too few companies: four startups give a low chance of catching a big winner, so his result depends heavily on luck.
3. Too fast: deploying everything in one year exposes him to whatever the market is paying today.
4. A disciplined version: set the budget at, say, 7.5% of ₹1.6 crore = ₹12 lakh; keep 30% (₹3.6 lakh) in reserve; use ₹8.4 lakh for initial cheques spread over four years.
5. The practical constraint: ₹8.4 lakh across 8 companies is only about ₹1.05 lakh each, which may be below some minimums. He can accept fewer companies, grow the portfolio as his budget grows, or look for syndicates with lower minimums. With ₹1.6 crore of net worth he is not an accredited investor, so new SEBI angel funds are not an option for him.
6. He should also review his children's education goals and home loan plans before committing, and treat his friend's success as one data point, not a forecast.

body.title: Name the pot
body.textWithBlank: Money held back from your angel budget to invest again in your best-performing companies is called follow-on ___.
body.explanation: Follow-on reserves let you use pro-rata rights in winners. A common range is 30 to 50% of the total angel budget.

cards.definition: Financial assets you control and could invest, excluding your own home and money earmarked for specific needs.
A commonly cited guardrail of around 5 to 10% of investable net worth in startups, with first-timers at the lower end.
Around 15 to 25 or more companies built over 3 to 5 years, to improve the odds of owning a winner.
Budget held back, often 30 to 50%, to invest in later rounds of the strongest companies.
Total budget × (1 − reserve %) ÷ number of companies.
Spreading initial cheques across several years so you invest through different valuation cycles.
When one successful investment grows to a much larger share of your wealth than planned.

points: Only start angel investing once your emergency fund, insurance, debt and core goals are in order, and only with money you can lose completely.
Set a total budget first; a commonly cited guardrail is 5 to 10% of investable net worth, lower for first-timers.
Back enough companies to give yourself a real chance at a winner; 15 to 25 or more over several years is common guidance.
Initial cheque = budget × (1 − reserve %) ÷ number of companies, with reserves often 30 to 50%.
If the maths gives cheques below deal minimums, back fewer companies, go slower or pool through an eligible fund; do not inflate the budget.
Spread cheques over 3 to 5 years, use reserves only for winners, and watch for a single success taking over your net worth.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not personalised investment or financial planning advice. Allocation percentages, portfolio sizes and reserve ratios are general rules of thumb, not recommendations for any individual. All people and figures are illustrative. Consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser to decide what, if anything, is appropriate for your situation.
